extraction.venue: Applied Sciences 12(11), 5499 (MDPI). Received 25 Mar 2022; accepted 24 May 2022; published 28 May 2022.
extraction.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY). Titled a systematic review, but the body is a single-environment benchmark of four pathfinding algorithms plus a descriptive literature comparison. No review protocol (databases, search strings, inclusion rules, paper counts) is reported.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: the entire extracted text file (1,811 lines, journal pages 1-30 including references 1-95), in chunks of about 400 lines. Annotation file read in full: 68 entries (67 highlights, 1 free-text note). Metadata hint confirmed against the PDF header; authors' full names added. No parts skipped.
extraction.identification: None. Descriptive benchmark: the same grids are fed to each algorithm and the outputs are ranked. There is no causal design, no controls for hardware or run-to-run variance, and no repeated trials. Theory section is a taxonomy (uninformed / informed-heuristic / metaheuristic), not a tested hypothesis.
extraction.theory: Taxonomy only. Pathfinding is split into uninformed (BFS, Dijkstra), informed/heuristic (A*, Greedy Best First, D* Lite, HPA*, JPS) and metaheuristic (GA, ACO) families, and static vs dynamic. The paper argues heuristic methods save time by pruning the search space (Sections 2, 3.2). No formal model is stated beyond the cost functions F(n)=G(n)+H(n) and the Table 2 complexity expressions.
extraction.research_question: Which of four pathfinding algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, Breadth First Search, Greedy Best First) performs best on 2D square grids of size 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles, in terms of execution time, total iteration blocks, computed blocks and shortest path length, so that game developers can choose one? Secondary: how do the families compare in the literature on memory and time (Table 5).
extraction.data: Synthetic game-style grids generated in the Unity engine: 2D square (octile) grids of 4x4, 8x8, 16x16 and 32x32 cells, each run with and without obstacles. Unit = one algorithm run on one grid configuration. Reported cells: 4 algorithms x 4 sizes x 2 conditions = 32 algorithm-by-grid results (16 rows in each of Tables 3 and 4). Not reported: number of repetitions, start and goal placement, obstacle layout or density, the iteration count k, hardware, and run dates. Literature input for Section 3 and Table 5: 95 references, span 1959 to 2022 (count of papers actually screened not stated). No real-world dataset.
extraction.method: Implemented BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First in Unity (Algorithms 1-4; the "GRIN_PF" Algorithm 6 is a harness that loops over these four). Per run recorded: total iteration blocks, total computed blocks excluding the shortest path, execution time in ms, and shortest path length in blocks (Section 5, p.19-20). Results compared as within-size rankings and narrative (Section 6, p.23-26). Theoretical side: asymptotic time/space table (Table 2, p.14) and a pairwise literature comparison table with category, time, memory, implemented yes/no, and cited source (Table 5, p.26-27). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or repeated timings. Memory was not measured.
extraction.scope: Population: single-agent pathfinding on regular 2D square grids in a game-style environment. Dynamic obstacles and 3D, hexagonal, triangular or irregular (waypoint, visibility graph, navmesh) grids are discussed but not tested. Institutions: VIT Chennai (India) and Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS (Malaysia); funded by YUTP grant 015LC0-134. Era: article 2022; cited literature 1959-2022. Not related to lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout or text measurement.

summary_md:
Lawande et al. (2022) call the paper a systematic review, but it is really a benchmark of four algorithms on one setup: BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First (GBF), each run once on Unity square grids from 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles. It reports no search protocol, no repeated trials, no hardware details and no measured memory, so its memory rankings and the Table 5 citations (several of which do not match the claims) cannot be relied on. The usable results are narrow. With no obstacles, GBF is fastest at every size; Dijkstra is 2.8x to 21.6x slower than GBF, and all four find the same path length. With obstacles, GBF stays fastest from 8x8 up, but its paths get longer (37 vs 31 at 16x16, 81 vs 75 at 32x32). A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra on the larger grids (587 vs 754 iterations at 32x32) and still returns the optimal length. D* and D* Lite are only described, never tested. The proposed GRIN_PF is just a loop that runs the four existing algorithms.

What this means for the system as built is mostly a check on design choices, not new evidence. The one sharp bearing comes from the paper's GBF-with-obstacles result. The dashboard's recruitment path first runs an exact max-product Dijkstra backward from the target (`distToTarget`), then walks forward greedily, choosing at each hop the neighbour with the highest edge probability times its precomputed reliability to the target. That walk is optimal only while the precomputed reliabilities are exact. Once a user drops members, the walk skips them but the reliabilities are still computed through them. The walk then becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate, which is the case where the paper shows longer, non-optimal paths. Terrier's walk router already does textbook A* with an admissible straight-line estimate, which is the setting where the paper's A* result applies best. For the non-spatial social graphs, the paper offers no usable heuristic.

bearings.paper_claim: Table 4 (with obstacles, single run): GBF is fastest from 8x8 up but its reported path is longer than the other three at 16x16 (37 vs 31 blocks) and 32x32 (81 vs 75). At 8x8 the table shows the reverse (GBF 13 vs 15 for the other three), an unexplained anomaly. Without obstacles all four report the same length (5/13/29/61, Table 3). The paper calls GBF 'not optimal'; it does not state the general rule that a greedy walk is optimal only when its estimate is exact (that is the analyst's inference).

bearings.system_side: distToTarget (line 734) runs an exact max-product Dijkstra from the target over the full PE graph and does not consult the dropped set. tracePath (line 740) walks forward greedily by argmax PE[cur][v]*dT[v], skipping seen and dropped nodes. With drops, dT can still reflect routes through excluded members, so the walk can return a less reliable chain or stop short ('unreachable') when a route exists. buildPath (753-757) and bestSponsors (760-764) reuse the same dT. The comment at line 735 says 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL'; dropped is set at line 1165. Single-path code reading, UNVERIFIED per DE-062.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the algorithmic point carries over (greedy choice on an inexact estimate loses optimality); grid timings and lengths do not. Cheap remedy is to exclude dropped members inside distToTarget. Needs a second-path reproduction (e.g. a test that drops a bridging member) before any claim.

summary_issues: The summary says that with obstacles GBF 'paths get longer', but Table 4 at 8x8 shows GBF reporting a SHORTER path than Dijkstra/A*/BFS (13 vs 15). This anomaly is unmentioned and undercuts the implicit claim that the other three always return the optimal length; the obstacle results are internally inconsistent at 8x8.

'A* ... still returns the optimal length' holds only relative to Dijkstra/BFS within this single run (equal lengths at 16x16 and 32x32); the paper never verifies optimality independently, and the 8x8 row casts doubt on it.

The recruitment-path drop finding is stated in the summary as fact ('The walk then becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate'); it is a single-path code reading and must carry the UNVERIFIED (DE-062) label in the summary too.
Bearing (not summary) error carried into the record: the staffer router's default search is bidirectional, not one-directional; the one-directional search is a test oracle only.

Other summary figures verified: Dijkstra/GBF time ratio without obstacles 39.7/14.38=2.76x to 7500.14/346.60=21.6x; 37 vs 31 and 81 vs 75; 587 vs 754; no protocol, no repeated trials, no hardware details (the paper itself says hardware performance is unknown), memory never measured.
gaps_exposed: The dashboard recruitment path (distToTarget at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:734) computes target reliabilities without excluding dropped members, while tracePath (line 740) skips them. With drops, the 'provably optimal' chain becomes a greedy walk on an out-of-date estimate. No test covers the case where a dropped member was on the route. Single-path observation, UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

There is no admissible estimate for the non-spatial social graphs (cosponsor, staffer), so A*-family speedups are not available there. ALT landmarks remain deferred. The paper's grid heuristics do not fill this gap.

No component replans incrementally (D*/D* Lite/LPA*) when the graph changes. For N=533 a full recompute is cheap enough. It would matter only for the multi-million-pair staffer graph, and the paper gives no evidence on that.
flags: The paper's memory rankings (GBF 'least memory', Dijkstra 'most memory usage') were never measured. Section 5 lists no memory metric. Do not cite this paper for memory claims.

The paper is not a systematic review (no protocol, databases or counts), and Table 5 cites references [90]-[95] that do not support the claims attached to them. Cite only the Table 3-4 counts, and label them single-run.
The GRIN_PF 'outperforms existing approaches' claim is untested. Do not cite it.

Wording: the dashboard comment calls the chain 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL ... mathematical certainty ... exact, maximal probability' (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-737). That holds only for the modeled kernel with no drops, and chainHold is a modeled output that depends on ASKM, not an empirical probability (D-025 spirit). The UI tooltip at line 1119 is already correctly hedged.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and says nothing about LDA or reciprocity. No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals.
paul_alignment: Paul files this paper in his Path-Finding folder as a citation only, with no takeaways. His only mark is the free-text note 'Very interesting' beside the D* node-state passage. The component positions also cite it as grounding for D*/D* Lite replanning (cosponsor-route-pareto) and as indirect support for Terrier's street routing. The evidence only partly supports that reading. The paper describes D* but never runs it, so it cannot ground the replanning layer Paul names in his addendum. Its tested contribution is narrower: A* beats Dijkstra on node expansions on larger grids when it has an admissible geometric estimate, and greedy search loses optimality once obstacles appear. Paul's note is not stale, since the system still has no incremental replanning. summary_md: Kumar, Mallik, Khetarpal and Panda (Information Sciences 607, 2022) propose SGNN, which treats influence maximization as a pseudo-regression task. Each node gets a struc2vec structural-identity embedding. A GNN regressor with LSTM neighbourhood aggregation is trained on labels made by simulating every node's individual spread under SIR and IC diffusion. The training network is chosen by a parametric sweep over synthetic graphs. The trained model then predicts node influence on an unseen target network, and the top-k predicted nodes become the seed set. The authors report that SGNN beats classical and recent IM baselines on several real networks under SIR and IC. The local text is only a ScienceDirect preview, so datasets, network sizes, metrics, effect sizes and limitations cannot be checked. Every performance claim here is the authors' own and is UNVERIFIED. The paper's stated motivation is cost: greedy IM is accurate and has a guarantee but is expensive, while centrality heuristics are cheap but network-specific. For Melange the cost argument mostly does not apply. The budget frontier already runs lazy (CELF-style) greedy with common random numbers on a single 533-member chamber graph and caps at 60 seeds, so the expensive side of the trade-off is affordable. Three features of SGNN also clash with choices Melange made on purpose. Seeds are ranked by each node's standalone spread, which ignores overlap between seeds. The embedding has no stance or direction, the same reason InfluenceScore was retired. And the labels come from single-colour diffusion, not the competitive two-colour race the engine models. The paper is best read as a scale-motivated alternative that Melange does not need, and as a caution against top-k standalone ranking.

extraction.research_question: How can the most reliable path, the path that maximizes the probability of arriving on time for a fixed travel-time budget, be found exactly and efficiently in large road networks with stochastic link travel times? (Abstract; Sec. 1, pp. 3-5.)
extraction.theory: Travel-time reliability is defined as the on-time arrival probability, P(T <= b), with path travel times treated as normal, so maximizing reliability is equivalent to minimizing z = (b - mean)/SD. The objective is non-additive, so Dijkstra-type methods do not apply. Solution logic rests on first-order stochastic dominance (FSD, Prop. 1), Mean-Budget (M-B) dominance (Prop. 3, from Chen et al. 2013a), and monotonicity of the objective under path extension (Lemmas 1-3). Risk-taking regimes (risk-averse, neutral, seeking) are set by the z-value of the least expected time path (Prop. 2, p. 8). No behavioral theory is tested empirically.
extraction.data: Case study on the Wuhan, China road network: 19,306 nodes and 46,757 links. Link travel times come from floating-car GPS data from 11,248 taxis reporting about every 40 seconds, map-matched with the MDP-MM algorithm, which the authors say reaches over 90% accuracy in prior work. Data cover five weekdays, 14-18 September 2009, 7-10 a.m. (Sec. 4.1, pp. 14-15). Unit of analysis: link and path travel times, and origin-destination (O-D) pairs. Link fits use chi-square tests at 5% across normal, lognormal and gamma distributions. Monte Carlo validation uses 100 randomly selected paths. Computational tests use 100 random O-D pairs per network, averaged over 100 runs, on four additional networks from Chen et al. (2013a): Chicago regional (12,982 nodes, 39,018 links), G1 (2,000 nodes, 7,820 links), G2 (5,000 nodes, 19,700 links), and G3 (10,000 nodes, 39,600 links). The paper does not report a count of O-D pairs for the single numerical example.
extraction.method: Two-stage exact algorithm, MRP-TS. Stage 1: a deterministic A* or Dijkstra search finds the least expected time path, which gives an upper or lower bound on the optimal reliability and sets the risk regime (Prop. 2). Stage 2: a multi-criteria label-setting procedure, MRP-RS for risk-seeking (fixed confidence level, Sec. 3.1) and MRP-RA for risk-averse (adaptive confidence level starting at 0.999, z = 3.5, with an admissible heuristic h(i), Sec. 3.2). Risk-neutral cases return the least expected time path directly. Optimality is argued through Props. 4-5 and Lemmas 1-3. Complexity is analyzed in Sec. 3.3. Benchmarks: the authors' improved multi-criteria label-correcting BSP-LC (Nie and Wu 2009 extended with a bi-criteria method, Appendix B, valid only for normal times), and multi-criteria A* from Chen et al. (2013a) used to check that MRP-TS returns the same paths. Implemented in Visual C#, one core of a 2.0 GHz i7 laptop, Windows 7. Identification strategy: not applicable; this is an algorithmic and computational paper with no causal design.
extraction.scope: Population: road travelers in a congested city network, modeled as a directed graph with stochastic link times. Institution: none. Era: data from 2009 morning peaks; paper published 2016. Geography: one Chinese city plus four synthetic or benchmark networks. Restrictions: road transport only; link travel times independent; O-D pairs randomly sampled; reliability computed in model terms, not validated against observed arrivals.

Chen, Shi, Zhang, Lam, Li and Xiang study a road-routing problem. Each link has a random travel time, and the goal is the path with the highest probability of arriving within a fixed time budget b, P(T <= b). They treat path times as normal, so this means minimizing (b - mean)/SD. Because path SD is the square root of summed variances, the objective is non-additive, and the authors state that Dijkstra-type methods cannot solve it. Their exact two-stage algorithm, MRP-TS, works as follows. A deterministic least-expected-time search first fixes the risk regime. Mean-Budget dominance with multi-criteria label-setting then finds the optimum. They check optimality by matching an independent multi-criteria A* on the same budgets. On Wuhan taxi data (19,306 nodes, 2009 morning peaks), the best path changes with b: a short budget picks a high-variance path and a long budget picks a low-variance one. MRP-TS runs in milliseconds, about 750x faster than the label-correcting benchmark on Chicago. Links are assumed independent, and the authors name correlation as the main open limitation.

What this means for Paul's system is narrow. The dashboard's recruitment chain (`make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-757`) cites this paper as grounding for its max-product path. That path is a different problem: the classical product-of-independent-probabilities path, which is additive in -log p and correctly solved by Dijkstra. This paper is about deadline-reliability, which is the case Dijkstra cannot handle. So the citation supports the word 'reliable', not the method. The paper's useful lessons are elsewhere. Exact optimality claims should be checked against a second algorithm, as Chen et al. do. Products of independent per-hop probabilities overstate certainty when the hops are correlated. And a true deadline or variance penalty on a recruitment chain would need label-setting, not Dijkstra. Nothing here concerns lobbying, legislators or elections.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's 'most reliable path' maximizes on-time arrival probability Phi((b - mean)/SD) for a travel-time budget b. It states that this objective 'is non-additive and cannot be solved by existing' shortest-path methods, so it uses M-B dominance plus multi-criteria label-setting (MRP-TS) rather than Dijkstra.

The code comment cites Chen, Shi, Zhang & Lam 2016 as grounding for 'maximize the probability the whole chain holds' and calls the result 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL'. A product of independent edge probabilities is additive in -log p (the Frank / Bellman reliable-path case), so Dijkstra is the right tool. That object is not the one this paper solves.

Sec. 2 notes the assumption can be relaxed with a two-level hierarchical network model (Chen et al. 2012); the Conclusions list correlation first among future directions, saying it is omitted "for simplicity" although urban link times are strongly correlated. Normal approximation of path travel time, checked against Monte Carlo ground truth on 100 randomly selected Wuhan paths, averages 98.3% accuracy at the 10th percentile and 94.9% at the 90th.

bearings.system_side: The chain is labelled 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL', but no second algorithm reproduces it. Agent reading (UNVERIFIED, DE-062): distToTarget(t) propagates d[v] = d[u]*PE[u][v] outward from the target, which is the reliability of target -> v. tracePath then walks sponsor -> target scoring PE[cur][v]*dT[v]. bearings.paper_claim: Penalizing path variability through SD makes the path objective non-additive, so Dijkstra loses exactness. Exact solutions need multi-criteria labels such as mean and variance.
bearings.system_side: The staffer router adds uncertainty linearly per hop: cost = -ln(0.8 x strength) + w x u, with u explicitly 'not a probability'. Because the penalty is a per-hop sum, bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 stays exact, and the code backs this with exact-arithmetic tie handling.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper serves as a boundary condition, not a criticism. The current additive design is correctly solved. If uncertainty were ever restated as an SD aggregated over the route, or as a probability of a usable introduction by a date, Dijkstra would no longer be exact and Chen-style label-setting would apply. Route costs remain heuristic outputs, never introduction or access probabilities (D-025).

summary_issues: Summary says the authors name correlation as "the main open limitation"; the paper lists it first among future research directions ("omitted in this study for simplicity"), not explicitly as the main limitation.

Bearing 2 location cited Sec. 1 for the independence assumption; it is in Sec. 2 and Sec. 5. Page numbers in several bearings were one page high relative to the extracted page-number lines (non-additivity p. 6 not 7; A* match p. 16 not 17).

Related link ren-2022 was described as the exact-front approach; Ren also presents a sub-optimal approximating variant. Related link lawande-2022 claimed Lawande reviews admissible heuristics; the word does not appear in its text. Both rewritten.
The distToTarget direction finding was re-read by this verifier and holds on code inspection, but it has not been executed against an exact solver; keep it UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
gaps_exposed: The recruitment chain has no time or deadline dimension. Chen shows that the best path depends on the budget b (risk-seeking at a short budget, risk-averse at a long one), but the system cannot express 'reach the target before markup or floor time' or choose a lower-variance chain when time is ample.

No second-path check backs the 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' recruitment-chain claim. Chen et al. validate MRP-TS against an independent multi-criteria A*; the dashboard has no exact solver to compare against (for example, a Dijkstra on -log p over directed PE with dropped nodes removed).

Agent finding, UNVERIFIED (DE-062): distToTarget propagates reliability from the target outward along forward edges, while tracePath needs v-to-target reliability. Under asymmetric PE (EMU receiver multipliers, role priors) the chain is not guaranteed optimal. The dropped set is also not applied in distToTarget, so a dropped node can make the walk stall when another path exists.

chainHold assumes the asks are independent. The source paper names independence as its main limitation, and recruitment asks along one chain are likely correlated, so the product is not a guaranteed floor.
The cosponsor-route Pareto front is approximate: five lambda scalarizations of a greedy, so non-supported Pareto points are missed. An exact dominance-based labeling is not built.
flags: Mis-grounding in code: make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-739 cites Chen, Shi, Zhang & Lam (Transportmetrica B 2016) as grounding for the max-product Dijkstra-on--log-p chain. That paper solves the non-additive on-time-arrival problem and says Dijkstra cannot solve it. The algorithm the code runs is the classical product-reliability path. The citation should be re-pointed (for example to Frank 1969 or classical reliable-path theory) or reworded. It does not support the method.

Over-claiming comment: tpl:736-737 calls the chain 'the mathematical certainty ... the exact, maximal probability of the optimal recruitment route'. The UI tooltip correctly says it is scenario output, not an empirical probability (tpl:1119). The comment should match, since chain reliability is a heuristic model output (in the spirit of D-025) built on an unestimated ASKM.

Bibliographic discrepancy in Paul's annotation: the citation reads vol. 5, no. 3, pp. 248-264, 13 Apr. 2016. The paper's own 'To cite' line gives vol. 5, pp. 253-269, 2017 print, online 13 Apr 2016; the issue number is not stated in the text.

No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues neither for dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor for per-edge volume normalization. It does not touch LDA (D-021) or reciprocity (D-104..D-108).
paul_alignment: Paul lists this paper with no takeaways, both in the Path-Finding Algorithums bibliography (citation only) and in the d963fd8719df reading list, where the only cross-reference is a title-level link to path choice under instability (Rongkuan 2024). His position for member-recruitment-path ('the built chain uses most-reliable-path Dijkstra and no learned heuristic') accurately describes the system. It also repeats the system's conflation: the built chain is a max-product reliable path, not Chen's deadline-reliability path, which Dijkstra cannot solve. His interest in coping with unstable or uncertain information is closer to what this paper actually offers: a budget-dependent, variance-aware route choice. That would need a time-to-join model the system does not have. His note is not stale about the code, but it inherits the code comment's mis-citation.

related.why: Ahmad's 'strongest path' over social-tie strengths is the classical max-product or -log-weight path that the dashboard chain actually implements. It is a better-fitting grounding for tpl:735-757 than Chen 2016.
Duan et al. speed up additive single-source shortest paths, which is the problem class the -log p chain and the staffer router belong to. Chen's objective is outside that class.

Both prune dominated partial paths with multi-criteria labels to get non-dominated path sets (MOPBD* path-based expansion vs M-B dominance label-setting). Ren also offers a sub-optimal variant that approximates the Pareto front, so it shows both the exact and approximate options relative to the lambda-scalarized front in cosponsor_route.py.

Lawande reviews heuristic pathfinding (A*, D*, HPA*). Chen's MRP-RA needs an admissible lower-bound heuristic for optimality (Prop. 5), which bears on Paul's wish for heuristic-augmented A* in the routers (both use heuristic 0). Lawande's text does not itself discuss admissibility.

It is co-cited with Chen 2016 in the same code comment (tpl:738-739) as the second grounding for the recruitment chain. Sotoudeh supplies the cosponsorship-influence edges and Chen is cited for the path objective.

extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (410 lines, about 18k chars) in one pass: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-6, both data sections, Tables 1-2, figure captions, and references. Nothing skipped. Topics touched: social search and path-finding, influence and tie strength in networks. Not present: lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout, allocation, text measurement. Annotation file read in full: 42 Highlight items by Paul Goff on pages 1-8, all with empty note text, so there are no sticky-note comments. Highlight colors are not interpreted.
extraction.research_question: Does using directed, weighted influence edges (capturing asymmetry and tie strength) make social-search paths from source to target more effective than the hop-count shortest path given by Dijkstra? (Sec. 1, p.1-2; Abstract)
extraction.theory: Influence of X on Y is the proportion of X's investment (interaction effort, time or count) directed at Y, normalized over all of X's investments; influence is asymmetric and lies between 0 and 1 (Sec. 3.1-3.3, p.3-4, citing Hangal et al. 2010 [5]). Tie strength from Granovetter's weak-ties argument motivates the weighting (Sec. 1.1, p.2). Global social search is treated as routing along the most influential path (Sec. 3, p.3).
extraction.data: Two datasets. (1) DBLP subset: about 38,942 unique author names and 16 data-mining conferences, January 2001 to February 2010; nodes are authors; undirected co-authorship edges weighted by co-authored papers (Sec. 5.1, p.6). (2) Twitter: 15 days of crawled tweets, about 23,491 unique users and 32,132 directed retweet edges; undated (Sec. 5.2, p.6). Experimental unit: 500 randomly selected source-destination pairs per dataset (Sec. 5.1, p.6). The Table 1 caption says "500 total nodes in the network", which conflicts with the stated network sizes; this is read here as the pair count, since the Table 1 counts sum to 500 per dataset.
extraction.method: Descriptive comparison of two path algorithms on the same source-destination pairs. Baseline: Dijkstra shortest path, measured by hop count, ties broken at random (Sec. 4, p.5; Sec. 5.1). Comparator: influence-based strongest path (Algorithm 1, from [5]), which enumerates candidate paths, multiplies edge influences along each path, and returns the path minimizing log(1/D) + log(1/product of influences) with D = 0.95 (p.5). Edge influence: DBLP = Papers(vi,vj)/sum_k Papers(vj,vk) (Eq. 2, p.6); Twitter = Retweets(Y,X)/sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z) (Eq. 3, p.6); general form Eq. 1 (p.4). Outcome measures: path length in hops and mean influence. No significance tests.
extraction.identification: None. No causal design, no randomized or quasi-experimental variation. The two algorithms are compared descriptively on the same sampled pairs.
extraction.scope: Population: DBLP authors in 16 selected data-mining conferences (2001-2010) and Twitter users in a 15-day undated window. Institutions: none studied. Era: 2001-2010 DBLP data; Twitter window undated. Generalization is claimed to "social networks" and "online social networks" (Abstract; Sec. 6) from two datasets only.

summary_md:
Ahmad, Ahmad and Vijay compare two ways of finding a social-search path between a source and a target. The first is plain Dijkstra, measured in hops. The second is the "strongest path" of Hangal et al. (2010). In that method, each directed edge carries an influence weight: the share of one node's total interaction investment that goes to the other node. The method then picks the path that minimises log(1/D) plus the log of 1 over the product of edge influences, with D = 0.95. The test uses 500 random source-target pairs in each of two networks: a DBLP co-authorship subset (2001-2010, about 38.9k authors) and a 15-day Twitter retweet graph (about 23.5k users, 32k directed edges). The strongest path was longer than the shortest in 64.6% of Twitter pairs and 45.0% of DBLP pairs. Mean lengths were 6.8 vs 4.9 hops on Twitter and 4.7 vs 3.3 on DBLP. The paper calls the weighted search "better", but it reports no measure of path quality, no outcome and no significance test. What it actually shows is only that the weighted route differs from the hop route and is longer. It is a method note, not evidence about legislatures.

For Paul's systems, it matters in three places:
- **Staffer closeness router.** Its hop cost, -ln(0.8 x strength), has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence), with D = 0.8 instead of 0.95. So this paper is a method source for that router, but it gives no validation of it.
- **Social interaction layer.** Its edge probability (events divided by the author's posting volume) is essentially the paper's Eq. 3 retweet influence. The layer then averages the two directions, which throws away the asymmetry the paper argues for.
- **Dashboard recruitment path.** The path matrix PE is directed, because receiver edge multipliers and role priors make it so. But the backward Dijkstra (distToTarget) multiplies edges in the forward direction away from the target. So the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is exactly max-product only when PE is symmetric. This is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Algorithm 1 (from [5], Hangal et al.) enumerates all paths, multiplies edge influences along each, and returns the path minimizing Total_influence = log(1/D) + log(1/product of edge influences), with D = 0.95. As printed, log(1/D) is added once per path, not per hop, so it is a constant that cannot change which path wins. Table 2: average strongest vs shortest path length 6.8 vs 4.9 hops (Twitter) and 4.7 vs 3.3 (DBLP), over 500 random pairs per dataset. No path-quality metric is reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 4, p.5 (Algorithm 1); Sec. 5.3 and Table 2, p.7
bearings.system_side: Hop cost = -ln(HOP_FACTOR x strength) + w x uncertainty_cost, with HOP_FACTOR = 0.8, i.e. ln(1/0.8) + ln(1/strength) per hop. The ln(1/strength) sum matches the paper's log(1/product) term. The per-hop ln(1/0.8) is a hop-length penalty with no counterpart in Algorithm 1 as printed, where log(1/D) is a per-path constant. Solved by bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, not by enumerating paths. Edges are undirected.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the log-inverse-product part of the objective carries over. The router's per-hop decay is its own design (possibly closer to Hangal's original paper, not checked here), not something Ahmad et al. print. The paper does not validate the objective: it never measures whether strongest paths succeed more often. Its influence is directed and normalized by investment; staffer strength is symmetric exposure. Route cost is a heuristic model output, not an introduction probability (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper text checked: D = 0.95, the Total_influence formula and the Table 2 numbers all match. But Algorithm 1 computes log(1/D) once per path, so calling the router's per-hop ln(1/0.8) 'the same per-hop decay' form is wrong for this paper. Code confirmed: lines 115-116 (_hop_cost), closeness_math.py:20 (HOP_FACTOR = .8), and the docstring at 3-21 (undirected edges, bidirectional Dijkstra, heuristic 0).

bearings.paper_claim: Influence is asymmetric: if Y is highly influenced by X, the reverse is not guaranteed, even for undirected interactions such as co-authorship (Sec. 3.2; Sec. 1.1). Asymmetry 'has to be considered' in social search; the paper does not say in so many words that edges must be directed. Average node influence is 0.67 (Twitter) and 0.60 (DBLP), and most node influence values lie below one (Sec. 5.3, Table 2).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1.1, p.2; Sec. 3.2, p.3; Sec. 5.3 and Table 2, p.6-7
bearings.system_side: ADJ is symmetric, but PEBASE[u][v] multiplies by the receiver's EMU[v], and configureIssueNetwork scales PE[u][v] by source_shock(u)/target_resistance(v), so PE is directed. distToTarget(t) relaxes d[v] = d[u] x PE[u][v] outward from t, so dT[v] is the best product along t -> ... -> v in the forward edge direction. tracePath scores sponsor -> target moves with PE[cur][v] x dT[v]. When PE is asymmetric, the chain the comment calls 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' is therefore not guaranteed to be the max-product sponsor-to-target chain. tracePath also skips 'dropped' nodes that distToTarget does not exclude, which is a second way the trace can depart from the optimum. UNVERIFIED single-path reading (DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's asymmetry point is enough to say edge direction matters for path search. The defect comes from reading the code, not from the paper. Its size depends on how far EMU (0.80-1.20) and the role priors push PE[u][v] away from PE[v][u], and on whether dropped nodes lie on the best chain. It may be small. A second path should confirm it (DE-062), for example by comparing Dijkstra on -log of the transposed PE with the traced chain.
bearings.verifier_note: The asymmetry statement is in Sec. 3.2 (and 1.1), not Sec. 3.3, and the paper does not say edges 'must be directed'. Wording corrected. 0.67/0.60 and 'below one' confirmed. Code confirmed at the cited lines: 547 symmetric ADJ, 586 EMU[v] in PEBASE, 594-597 source/target role priors, 734 forward-direction relaxation from the target, 740 tracePath with the dropped-node skip. The asymmetry argument holds on reading. Added the dropped-node caveat.

bearings.paper_claim: Twitter influence(X,Y) = Retweets(Y,X) / sum_Z Retweets(Y,Z): the share of Y's retweets that go to X. This is a directed weight normalized by the retweeter's total retweet volume (Eq. 3). The paper's reason for directed weights is that influence is asymmetric (Sec. 3.2).
bearings.system_side: p(a->b) = weighted events(a->b) / max(25, posts(a)), capped at 0.25 per direction. Events are reposts (1.0) and mentions (0.4); posts(a) counts all of a's Quorum posts, not only reposts, and excludes Bluesky. This is a per-author volume normalization like Eq. 3, but the denominator is total posts rather than total retweets. The pair weight is then the mean of the two directions, and only a 'symmetric' edge list is written, so direction is discarded.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is descriptive: a 15-day undated Twitter crawl in which strongest paths are longer, with no outcome. It does not show that directed retweet edges predict anything legislative. At most it gives weak support for keeping a directed variant of this layer alongside the symmetric one before path or recruitment use. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project's SNA tests: do not read this as support for wider volume normalization.
bearings.verifier_note: The form of Eq. 3 is confirmed. 'The same per-author volume normalization as Eq. 3' was overstated: the layer divides by all posts (floor 25) and mixes in 0.4-weighted mentions, while Eq. 3 divides by total retweets. The cap applies per direction before averaging (line 56). Mean of directions (line 61) and symmetric-only output (67-69) confirmed. Asymmetry is Sec. 3.2, not 3.3.

bearings.paper_claim: Hop-count shortest paths ignore tie strength and asymmetry (Abstract). Tie strength matters for social search (Granovetter motivation, Sec. 1.1). The strongest path uses the product of normalized influences (Sec. 4).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract, p.1; Sec. 1.1, p.2; Sec. 4, p.5
bearings.system_side: Overlap routes minimize summed integer distances plus one balanced unit (DISTANCE_SCALE) per introduction. There are two cost forms. Shared-background mode uses ceil(1e6 x 128 / strength), with strength = sum(weight x log2(1 + shared facts)). Work-time mode uses ceil(1e6 / strength), with strength = proximity x log2(1 + overlap days / 30). Both are additive inverse strengths, not -log of a bounded weight, so neither can be read as a product of per-hop reliabilities.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Context only. The paper does not compare inverse-strength costs with log-product costs, and the overlap router is a deliberate design choice. Shared work days and shared background are heuristic tie scores, not measures of closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). Influence language is barred on revolving-door edges.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds. The code side conflated two modes. The 128-scaled cost (line 34) goes with the shared-facts strength (line 331 provenance). The log2(1 + days/30) work-time strength (line 39) goes with ceil(1e6 / strength) at line 211. The conclusion (additive inverse strengths, not log-product) holds for both.

summary_issues: The summary says the closeness router's hop cost -ln(0.8 x strength) 'has the same form as Hangal's per-hop log(1/D) + log(1/influence)'. In the paper's Algorithm 1, log(1/D) is added once per path, not per hop, so it cannot change which path wins. Only the log(1/product of influences) part is shared. The router's per-hop ln(1/0.8) is a length penalty the paper does not print.

The summary says the social layer's edge probability is 'essentially the paper's Eq. 3'. Eq. 3 divides by the retweeter's total retweets. The layer divides by the author's total Quorum posts (floor 25), adds 0.4-weighted mentions, and caps each direction at 0.25. It is a similar per-author volume normalization, not the same one.

The summary says the recruitment chain is exactly max-product 'only when PE is symmetric'. Symmetry is necessary but not sufficient: tracePath also skips 'dropped' nodes that distToTarget does not exclude. The finding stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

The related link to steinertthrelkeld-2018-twitter-data was removed. That item's own extraction says the book never discusses reposts, mentions, edge probabilities or normalization, so it does not cover the retweet-influence definition used here.

The related link to chen-2016-most-reliable-path claimed the same objective. Chen maximizes on-time arrival probability under stochastic travel times, not a product of edge probabilities. The link holds only through the dashboard's citation.
gaps_exposed: The recruitment path's backward Dijkstra does not transpose a directed PE. Nothing checks that the 'provably optimal' chain is optimal when receiver and role multipliers make edges asymmetric (UNVERIFIED; needs a second path).
The social interaction layer computes directed probabilities but publishes only their mean. No directed social edge reaches path search or recruitment.

No router (member recruitment, staffer closeness or staffer overlap) has an outcome log against which 'strongest' and 'shortest' routes could be compared. The paper never measured this either, so the strongest-vs-shortest question stays open in both.
flags: The paper's influence weight (an edge divided by the actor's total investment) is a volume normalization. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project's SNA tests: cite the paper as a method description only, never as grounds to extend volume normalization to the cosponsor or staffer graphs.

The paper's claims that 'it is proved' and 'better result' (Abstract; Sec. 6) rest only on path-length differences over 500 pairs, with no outcome or test. Do not quote them as validation of any router.

The Table 1 caption says '500 total nodes in the network', which conflicts with the stated network sizes; read it as 500 pairs. Any figure quoted from the paper must name the window (DBLP 2001-2010; Twitter 15 days, undated) and the denominator (500 pairs).
The dashboard-path asymmetry finding is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Route costs and strengths are heuristic model outputs, not introduction or access probabilities (D-025).
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights centre on the asymmetric definition of influence, the comparison between Dijkstra and the strongest path, and the conclusion that weighted search beats unweighted search. He left no notes, and his positions list Ahmad only under member-recruitment-path, as the strongest-path citation. The system partly matches that reading. The staffer closeness router uses the Hangal objective form, with D = 0.8. The recruitment path uses a most-reliable (max-product) Dijkstra, which follows Chen 2016 more closely than Ahmad. Where the system departs from the asymmetry Paul highlighted: the social layer averages away direction, and the recruitment path's backward pass does not respect PE's direction. Paul's highlighted line about "better result" goes further than the evidence, since the paper measures only path length. His takeaway should be held as a method preference, not as a validated finding.

related.why: The dashboard recruitment path cites Chen et al. 2016 for its max-product ('most reliable') chain, the same objective Ahmad et al. call the strongest path. Chen's own objective is different: it maximizes on-time arrival probability under stochastic link travel times, not a product of edge probabilities.
Both treat tie strength (Granovetter) and direction as core tie properties. Paul cites Haythornthwaite for directionality, and in the staffer-closeness-routes and SNA components.

Directed single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights. An exact strongest-path search (Dijkstra on -log influence) could use this in place of Ahmad's exhaustive path enumeration. Both are cited for member-recruitment-path.
Compares Dijkstra with A*, BFS and greedy best-first on grids, which includes the Dijkstra baseline used here. Both are cited for member-recruitment-path.

backlinks.why: Strongest-path search over social tie strength corresponds to the review's trust-propagation operators and path-length decay concern.
Both turn tie strength into path cost for shortest-path search. Zeller adds a way to fit that transform empirically (used vs available paths) rather than setting it by hand.

meta.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users

extraction.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users
extraction.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0), 11 pages
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks, from title page through the author-contributions and licence page (text file 41,391 chars, 841 lines). Metadata hint is correct; no correction needed. All 38 items in the annotation file (_annots/a6421bb84f3f.json) were read. Every item is a Highlight by Paul Goff, with no sticky notes, typed comments or note text. Highlight colours: 1 green (0.49, 0.78, 0.41) and 37 yellow (0.98, 0.80, 0.35). Several highlights overlap and their covered text is interleaved, so fragments are marked [...]. Topic check: the paper covers networks, path-based (semi-local) similarity indices and link prediction. It contains no content on lobbying, allocation, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement.
extraction.research_question: Can similarity scores for link prediction that go beyond common first-order neighbours (through a latent relationship captured by the correlation of second-order neighbourhood profiles) predict missing or future links more accurately than eight established similarity baselines?
extraction.theory: No named social theory. The premise is that structural similarity between two nodes predicts link formation (pp.1-2, citing Ke-ke et al. / Shang et al., ref 18). Common neighbours are treated as an incomplete measure, and a latent relationship is defined as indirect connectivity through second-order neighbours (p.2). Hypothesis 1: if two nodes with a future link have no common neighbour but a significant latent relationship, the link can be predicted. Hypothesis 2: latent relationships separate existing from non-existing links even when pairs share the same number of common neighbours (p.4).
extraction.data: Nine static real-world networks, each treated as one snapshot with no time dimension (Table 1, p.8): KRT Zachary karate club (34 nodes, 78 edges, social); DLN dolphins (62, 159, animal); UAL US airline traffic (332, 2126, airport traffic); NSC NetScience co-authorship (379, 914); INF face-to-face contacts at an exhibition (410, 2765); EML Rovira i Virgili email (1133, 5451); YST yeast biological network (2284, 6646); HAM Hamsterster social network (2426, 16630); KHN co-authorship (3772, 12718). Unit of analysis: node pairs (existing edges and non-existing pairs). No collection period is stated. Each network's sample is the full network as published, with no sampling step described.
extraction.method: Similarity-based link prediction. For each node i, a neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10, p.6) has entries d_i at the node itself, CN_iz for second-order neighbours, CN_iz + 1 for first-order neighbours, and 0 otherwise. The union set UN_ij (Eq. 11) is the set of indices where either vector is positive. The indirect similarity Corr_ij is the Pearson correlation of N_i and N_j over UN_ij (Eqs. 12-13). The DICN score is DICN_ij = (1 + CN_ij)(1 + Corr_ij) (Eq. 14, p.7). Algorithm 1 (p.6) gives the pseudo-code. Evaluation: edges are randomly split into a training set (beta = 80% by default, 50-90% swept in Exp. 2) and a test set; the process is repeated 15 times and averaged. AUC (Eq. 15, pp.7-8) is computed by comparing every test edge with every non-existing pair, counting ties as 0.5. Eight baselines were implemented in Java: CN, PA, JC, HPI, CNDP, NCC, CCPA and SHOPI.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is out-of-sample link prediction using random edge holdout. Hypotheses 1 and 2 are tested by restricting test and non-existing pairs to subsets defined by common-neighbour status (Exp. 3 and Exp. 4, pp.9-10).
extraction.scope: Population: nine public real-world networks of mixed type (social, animal, airline, co-authorship, contact, biological, email), all treated as static. The paper does not claim a broader population. Era: not stated; published 2020. The paper names directed and weighted networks as future work (p.10), which implies none were analysed.

key_findings.finding: Common neighbours miss many links: a share of existing edges have no common neighbour. Shares range from 3.1% (UAL) to 53.7% (YST).

Existing and non-existing links overlap heavily at the same common-neighbour count, so the count alone separates them poorly. Fig. 2 shows the overlap, with roughly an even split near 8 common neighbours for INF, EML and YST.
key_findings.numbers: around 8 common neighbours (INF, EML, YST); no tabulated values in the text

key_findings.finding: Proposed DICN score combines direct similarity (common neighbours) with indirect similarity (Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors). Worked examples: Corr_25 about -0.74 gives DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_38 about 0.32 and Corr_31 about 0.01 for the Fig. 3 pairs.
key_findings.numbers: DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_25 about -0.74; Corr_38 about 0.32; Corr_31 about 0.01

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1 (beta = 80): DICN has the highest AUC in eight of nine networks. In UAL it is close to the best but not the best.
key_findings.numbers: DICN vs best other: KRT 0.7654 vs 0.7336 (CNDP); DLN 0.7943 vs 0.7570 (CCPA); UAL 0.9367 vs 0.9416 (NCC); NSC 0.9747 vs 0.9195 (CNDP); INF 0.9553 vs 0.9483 (CCPA); EML 0.8932 vs 0.8729 (SHOPI); YST 0.8278 vs 0.7892 (CCPA); HAM 0.9725 vs 0.9617 (CCPA); KHN 0.8839 vs 0.8509 (SHOPI)

key_findings.finding: Experiment 2 (beta swept 50-90): DICN is consistently best for beta of 70 or higher in seven of nine networks. It is not always best at small training fractions, which the authors attribute to weaker detectable correlation.
key_findings.numbers: seven of nine networks at beta >= 70; Fig. 5 values not given in text

key_findings.finding: Experiment 3 (Hypothesis 1, pairs with no common neighbours and degree > 1): among PA, CCPA, SHOPI and DICN, DICN is best in five networks and close to the best in the other four.
key_findings.numbers: DICN best: KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471, EML 0.7595, HAM 0.7831, KHN 0.8001. Others: DLN 0.7028 vs CCPA 0.7211; UAL 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8091; INF 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8404; YST 0.7609 vs PA 0.7755

key_findings.finding: Experiment 4 (Hypothesis 2, pairs with equal common-neighbour counts; compared with NCC, CNDP, CCPA, SHOPI): DICN is best in five networks, near the best in three, and clearly worst in UAL.
key_findings.numbers: DICN best: NSC 0.7815, INF 0.7712, EML 0.7495, HAM 0.7483, KHN 0.7829. Near best: KRT 0.6728 vs SHOPI 0.6919; DLN 0.6508 vs CCPA 0.6510; YST 0.7595 vs CCPA 0.7613. UAL: DICN 0.5684 vs SHOPI 0.7921

key_findings.finding: AUC worked example: with five non-existing edges and one test edge (DICN_35 = 2.5), n1 = 3 and n2 = 1 give AUC = 0.7. The AUC formula is (n1 + n2/2)/n.
Motivating example: CN gives S_24 = 1 > S_45 = 0, yet nodes 4 and 5 may share a latent relationship via their neighbours 2 and 3.

measures: AUC (Eq. 15, pp.7-8), the evaluation metric
Common Neighbours (CN, Eq. 1)
Preferential Attachment (PA, Eq. 2)
Jaccard Index (JC, Eq. 3)
Hub Promoted Index (HPI, Eq. 4)
Common Neighbours Degree Penalization (CNDP, Eq. 5)
Node-coupling Clustering (NCC, Eq. 6)
Parameterized Algorithm (CCPA, Eq. 7)
Significance of Higher-Order Path Index (SHOPI, Eqs. 8-9)
DICN (proposed): (1 + CN)(1 + Pearson correlation of neighbourhood vectors), Eq. 14
Neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10) and union neighbourhood set UN_ij (Eq. 11)
limitations: Stated by the authors: when the training set is small, the latent relationship is harder to detect because the correlation is lower, so DICN may be less accurate (p.9).
Stated by the authors: in UAL, and in Exp. 4 more generally, NCC, CNDP and SHOPI significantly outperform DICN (p.10).
Stated by the authors: the latent relationship is restricted to second-order neighbours; extending it to path counts or node centrality is future work (p.10).
Stated by the authors: directed and weighted networks, and more varied networks, are future work (p.10).
Reviewer observation (not stated by the authors): AUC is the only metric. No standard deviation or significance test across the 15 random splits is reported, only averages.
Reviewer observation: the Experiment 3 text calls the four non-DICN-best networks 'very close' to the best, but the INF gap is 0.8404 vs 0.7979 (SHOPI vs DICN).
Reviewer observation: the self-entry d_i is part of the vector and therefore enters the Pearson correlation (Eq. 10). The effect of degree on Corr_ij is not separately examined.
Reviewer observation: the paper gives 8 MB memory for the test machine (p.7). This is probably a typo for GB, but the text reads 8 MB as printed.

summary_md:
Zareie and Sakellariou propose DICN, a link-prediction score that multiplies a direct term (1 + common neighbours) by an indirect term (1 + the Pearson correlation of two nodes' neighbourhood vectors, which include second-order neighbours). They motivate it with two observations. First, between 3.1% (UAL) and 53.7% (YST) of existing edges join nodes that share no common neighbour. Second, at the same common-neighbour count, linked and unlinked pairs overlap heavily. They test it on nine small, static, unweighted, undirected networks, holding out 20% of edges at random over 15 repeats and scoring with AUC only. DICN has the highest AUC in 8 of 9 networks. The margins over the best baseline range from about 0.01 (INF, HAM) to about 0.055 (NSC), and DICN loses on UAL. It also wins in 5 of 9 networks on pairs with no common neighbour, and in 5 of 9 on pairs with equal common-neighbour counts, where it is clearly worst on UAL (0.568 vs 0.792). No variances or significance tests are reported. Weighted and directed graphs are left to future work.

For Melange, the paper is a candidate source of dyadic features, not evidence about influence. The sharpest use is in the ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster. Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count. Every other network term describes a single node (degree, eigenvector), so common-neighbour and second-order similarity between the sponsor and the candidate are missing. The press HCoI layer already uses the correlation-of-profiles idea through Malaterre, but it uses correlation alone, without the direct term. Any DICN-style score in this system is a heuristic similarity output, not closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). It stays UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced under the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: DICN = (1 + CN)(1 + Corr), where Corr is the Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors. At beta = 80% training it has the highest mean AUC (15 random splits) in 8 of 9 networks (e.g. NSC 0.9747 vs CNDP 0.9195; KHN 0.8839 vs SHOPI 0.8509). It loses on UAL (0.9367 vs NCC 0.9416). On test pairs whose nodes share no common neighbour (Exp. 3, compared only with PA, CCPA and SHOPI), it is best in 5 of 9 networks (e.g. KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471).

bearings.system_side: The forecaster scores (bill, member) candidates with ridge logistic regression on prior-Congress HR/S features. The only dyadic feature drawn from the cosponsor graph is the direct prior member-to-sponsor affinity count and rate. The other dyadic terms are attribute-based: same party, state and chamber, NOMINATE distances, and an optional prior committee co-service term. Prior degree and eigenvector centrality are member-level and are computed on an undirected weighted sponsor-cosponsor projection. There is no common-neighbour, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar or second-order similarity feature between sponsor and candidate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper uses random edge holdout on nine static benchmark graphs (34-3,772 nodes) that it does not describe as weighted or directed; it lists those as future work. The forecaster is temporal (the Congress t-1 graph predicts Congress t joins) and bill-level. Its prior graph is an undirected weighted projection, and its affinity feature is ordered (member, sponsor). Paper margins over the best baseline run from about 0.007 to 0.055 AUC, with no variance reported. A sponsor-candidate CN or DICN feature on the prior-Congress graph is a cheap candidate to test against the affinity baseline. Exp. 3 concerns pairs with no common neighbour, which is a different subset from pairs with zero direct prior affinity, so it should not be read as evidence about zero-affinity pairs. Any lift is UNVERIFIED until shown on the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers match the text (Table 2 lines ~515-584 and Table 3 line ~635-650 of the text file; 'eight of the nine' p.9; 'five of the nine' Exp. 3). Code: CONTINUOUS_FEATURES at 117-140 confirmed. Corrections: (1) prior_committee_coservice is also a dyadic feature, though not graph-derived, and same_party/state/NOMINATE distance are dyadic attributes. (2) The prior network is an undirected weighted projection (network_definition string in compute_prior_statistics), not a directed graph. (3) The analyst equated Exp. 3 'no common neighbour' pairs with zero-affinity pairs; these are different subsets.

bearings.system_side: HCoI builds member-member edges purely from Pearson correlation of recency-weighted 19-category press-attention profiles (threshold HCOI_CORR = 0.6, minimum weight 3.0). It then runs Louvain with seed 7 and reports how many cosponsor-isolated members (D4) land in a community. It does not combine the correlation with any direct cosponsor tie.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The analogy is loose. HCoI correlates topic-attention profiles, not neighbourhood vectors. The transferable point is a design point: in DICN the profile correlation is one factor, anchored on direct shared ties. Placing cosponsor-isolated members (D4) by correlation alone is loosely analogous to Exp. 3 (no common neighbours), but that is still a heuristic placement, not evidence of a relationship (D-025).

summary_issues: The summary calls the nine networks 'unweighted, undirected'. The paper never states this directly; it lists directed and weighted networks as future work. Wording should say 'treated as static, with directed and weighted graphs left to future work'.

'Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count' is slightly overstated. Affinity is the only cosponsor-graph dyadic feature, but the forecaster also has dyadic attribute features (same party, state and chamber, NOMINATE distances) and an optional prior committee co-service term. Degree and eigenvector come from an undirected weighted projection.
The margin range 'about 0.01 (INF, HAM)' is rounded. INF's actual margin is 0.007 (0.9553 vs CCPA 0.9483). The NSC figure (0.055) is correct.
Bearing text elsewhere attributes UAL's loss to hub-dominated structure. The paper gives no such reason, and the summary should not import it.

System facts cited in the bearings but absent from the cited code have been removed in verification: 77% masking sign agreement, null co-movement, null HCoI homophily, +/-0.15 valence colour thresholds, and co-appearance described as 'display only'. They remain UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
Relation to Malaterre was labelled 'same-method'. It is a shared technique (Pearson profile correlation) on different inputs, so it was downgraded to 'complements'.
gaps_exposed: The cosponsor forecaster has no sponsor-candidate structural-similarity feature (common neighbours, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, or second-order correlation). Its only dyadic network signal is direct prior affinity, so pairs with zero prior history get only node-level and ideology terms.

No link-prediction benchmark exists in the system. The engine kernel, recruitment paths and cascades treat a missing cosponsor tie as p = 0, with no estimate of how many ties are merely unobserved. The paper finds that up to 53.7% of edges lack common neighbours in some networks.

There is no evaluation of any system tie-inference layer (HCoI correlation edges, co-appearance) as a predictor of later cosponsor ties by AUC under a temporal holdout. The paper's evaluation protocol (AUC with ties counted as 0.5, Eq. 15) is a ready template, adapted to temporal rather than random splits.
flags: D-025: any DICN or common-neighbour score added to the system is a heuristic similarity output. It must never be described as closeness, access or introduction probability.

Rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues for neither dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization. However, DICN is defined only on unweighted graphs, so a naive port would binarize the cosponsor graph and erase the 1.0/0.5 original/regular distinction. Do not let a DICN port quietly re-introduce the rejected edge changes; compute it on the existing graph or a documented weighted extension.

Component list mismatch: Zareie & Sakellariou 2020 is listed as a citation for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references, which concerns negative or signed ties. The paper is unsigned and gives no basis for negative-tie handling.
Paul filed the paper under 'Path-Finding Algorithums'. It is a link-prediction (similarity) paper with no path-finding content.

Evidence quality: the only metric is AUC, averaged over 15 random splits, with no variance or significance tests and static benchmark graphs. Any system use is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul left no takeaway for this paper. Both bibliography entries are citation-only, and his PDF markup is 38 plain highlights with no notes. The highlights focus on the claim that common neighbours alone are insufficient, the neighbourhood-vector and correlation construction, and the no-common-neighbour experiment. The paper supports that emphasis, but the gains are modest (about 0.01-0.05 AUC) and come from small, static, unweighted benchmarks. Filing it under path-finding understates its real use: it supplies dyadic similarity features for link and cosponsor prediction. The component list also cites it for negative ties in the co-appearance and reference layers, which it does not address. Nothing in his notes is stale against the built system, because the system never adopted this method. The closest built analogue is HCoI's profile correlation, which came from Malaterre, not from this paper.

related.why: Malaterre infers ties from Pearson correlation of LDA topic profiles at a 0.6 threshold and then runs Louvain, the recipe press_hcoi.py implements. Zareie also uses Pearson correlation, but on structural neighbourhood vectors, and multiplies it by a direct common-neighbour term. The overlap is technique-level, not the same method.
Signed (positive and negative) link prediction covers the negative-tie question for the reference layer, which Zareie's unsigned similarity does not address.
Predicts negative links from positive links and interaction content (Epinions, Slashdot), which fills the signed-tie gap this method leaves open.
Builds undirected, weighted, time-decayed House cosponsorship graphs. A DICN-style dyadic feature would have to be adapted to that weighted setting, which Zareie leaves to future work.
Same authors. A narrative survey of behaviour-aware influence-maximization methods, the downstream use of tie estimates in cascade models.
